ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns, though presenters speak in long, highly structured monologues. Early conversation is informal and chatty, with greetings, technical check-ins, side remarks, laughter-like reactions, and frequent fillers such as “yeah,” “um,” “okay,” and “right.” Speakers often self-correct, restart phrases, repeat words, and use tentative framing (“I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “you know,” “I guess”), especially when speculating. Interruptions are limited during formal talks but overlap lightly in transitions and question periods; questions often begin with praise or disclaimers like “quick question,” “naive question,” or “great talk,” then develop into multi-part, exploratory prompts. Disagreement is indirect and collaborative, expressed through caveats, alternative explanations, or requests for clarification rather than blunt contradiction. Participants build on one another by referencing a prior point, paraphrasing it, and extending it with a related question or suggestion. Formality rises noticeably during introductions and presentations, but even then the delivery remains conversational, with repeated transitions, audience-oriented signposting, and occasional joking or personal asides.

Meeting style for this meeting (running_out_of_time): The meeting starts late or the agenda is too long. People keep an eye on the clock, cut themselves off, skip items, and the meeting ends with things unfinished. No final recap.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - We've got maybe fifteen minutes, so- can we skip the intro stuff?
  - Yeah, sure. Let's just start with what's blocking.
  - I really have to jump in about five, sorry.
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Working out why wild bee numbers on farms did not recover after wildflower strips were planted along field edges.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Rahman
speakers.background: A landscape ecologist with six years of postdoctoral and doctoral research on farmland biodiversity in mixed arable systems. She has designed before-after-control-impact studies, mapped semi-natural habitat and hedgerow networks using GIS, and analyzed repeated insect-survey data with hierarchical mixed models. Her recent work examines how floral resources interact with nesting habitat, field configuration, and weather variation across years.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats the strips as one component of a wider ecological network rather than a self-contained intervention. She will press the group to distinguish a local strip effect from differences in surrounding habitat, connectivity to source populations, availability of nesting resources, and year-to-year weather or population variation. She favors a multi-year, replicated design with planted and carefully matched unplanted edges across farms, paired with landscape mapping and repeated surveys. She sees the existing transects, seed-mix records, management dates, and farm locations as useful starting material, but will flag that stronger inference needs broader spatial replication and pre-specified comparison scales.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Tomás Iversen
speakers.background: A pollinator biologist and field-methods engineer with nine years of experience supporting bee-monitoring projects for universities and agricultural advisory groups. He has run pan-trap and transect protocols, trained field teams in species-level identification, assessed nesting substrates, and coordinated pollen, residue, and laboratory exposure assays. His work includes comparing responses of bumblebees, solitary bees, and hoverflies to floral-resource schemes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Tomás is concerned that total wild-bee counts can conceal opposite responses among species with different body sizes, nesting habits, seasonal activity, and foraging ranges. He will argue for species-level or at least functional-group identification, alongside measures that indicate how bees are using the strips, such as flower visitation, pollen use, occupancy, mark-recapture or other movement-focused approaches where feasible, and targeted nesting-resource assessments. He will want pesticide application logs linked to crop timing, active ingredients, and likely exposure pathways, then tested with feasible field residue sampling or carefully selected laboratory assays for sublethal effects. He treats the logs as a valuable exposure history, but not as direct evidence of dose or biological effect without additional measurement.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Leila M. Okafor
speakers.background: An agricultural economics PhD candidate in her fourth year, studying agri-environment scheme uptake and management intensity on commercial farms. She has conducted structured farmer interviews, built partial-budget and whole-farm cost models, analyzed farm-account records, and used discrete-choice experiments to test how payment design affects land-use decisions. Her current research focuses on heterogeneity in opportunity costs across field locations and farm types.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Leila frames strip placement and upkeep as endogenous farm decisions, not neutral implementation details. She will emphasize that marginal land values, foregone crop revenue, maintenance labor, machinery constraints, yield spillovers, and perceived agronomic risk can all shape where strips are placed and how consistently they are managed. A flat payment may therefore select sites with low opportunity cost or insufficiently reward strips in ecologically valuable but costly locations. She will propose combining existing financial records, crop rotations, management dates, and spatial field information with farmer interviews and partial-budget analysis; a larger study could add stated-preference or discrete-choice work and model differentiated, results-based, or location-weighted incentives. She will be forceful about measuring behavioral and financial constraints rather than treating compliance as uniform, while accepting that economic evidence must be integrated with ecological and exposure data.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

meeting_opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with enough research context for the evaluated AI to identify helpful methods from each discipline. Proposed reference methods must fit both the discipline and the research problem; expert review is needed.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give an interdisciplinary meeting with enough research context for the evaluated AI to identify helpful methods from each discipline. Proposed reference methods must fit both the discipline and the research problem; expert review is needed.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a planning meeting among an ecologist, a bee biologist, and an agricultural economist. The ecologist should describe the need to separate strip effects from landscape context, connectivity, nesting resources, and year-to-year variation, and should raise a multi-year design using planted and matched unplanted edges across farms. The biologist should explain that aggregate counts may hide species-specific responses and should identify the need for species-level identification, measures linked to foraging range or movement, nesting-resource assessment, and evaluation of sublethal pesticide exposure using the existing application logs plus appropriate field or laboratory measures. The economist should explain that farmer choices about placement and upkeep may be shaped by opportunity costs, maintenance costs, crop-yield effects, and the uniform subsidy, and should propose methods to quantify those trade-offs and assess alternative incentive designs. Participants should connect methods across disciplines where appropriate, identify feasible use of existing records, and distinguish methods that require additional data collection. They may recommend methods but must not claim that a particular method will prove the cause before expert review. The meeting should end with a provisional integrated study approach and unresolved design details such as sampling scale, sample size, and feasibility of exposure testing.

ecology.method: Replicated before-after-control-impact or difference-in-differences field design using planted strips and matched unplanted field edges, measured over multiple years.
ecology.fit: Separates change associated with strip establishment from baseline differences, annual variation, and broader farm trends.

ecology.method: Landscape-scale GIS analysis of semi-natural habitat, floral-resource distribution, field configuration, and connectivity around each strip at multiple biologically justified buffer sizes.
ecology.fit: Tests whether isolated strips or low-connectivity landscapes limit colonization or use by bees.

ecology.method: Standardized repeated bee surveys combined with floral-resource and nesting-resource surveys at strips, controls, and surrounding habitat.
ecology.fit: Links abundance patterns to local forage quality and nest-site availability rather than treating flower cover alone as habitat quality.

ecology.method: Hierarchical mixed-effects or occupancy/abundance models accounting for repeated visits, farm and year effects, weather, and imperfect detection.
ecology.fit: Provides an appropriate analysis for repeated ecological observations and heterogeneous farms.

biology.method: Species-level identification, potentially supported by voucher specimens and DNA barcoding for difficult taxa, followed by trait- or species-specific analyses.
biology.fit: Determines whether overall abundance masks losses, nonresponse, or replacement among species with different habitat needs.

biology.method: Trait-based analysis using foraging range, nesting guild, sociality, and floral specialization, with targeted sampling of representative species.
biology.fit: Tests whether strips fail for species unable to reach them or lacking required nesting resources.

biology.method: Pesticide-exposure assessment that links application timing, active ingredients, and treated crops to bee sampling, supplemented where feasible by residue analysis of pollen, nectar, or bee-relevant matrices.
biology.fit: Assesses whether exposure could suppress survival, reproduction, navigation, or foraging despite available flowers.

biology.method: Sublethal-effect assays or sentinel/field-colony measures selected with toxicology expertise, such as foraging activity, brood development, or condition measures.
biology.fit: Evaluates biological mechanisms that simple adult transect counts can miss.

economics.method: Farm-level enterprise budgets and partial-budget analysis for strip establishment, maintenance, foregone cropped land, and crop-yield changes near strips.
economics.fit: Quantifies the private costs and benefits that may influence strip placement and maintenance quality.

economics.method: Econometric analysis of farm records and management choices, with careful treatment of non-random strip placement and farm heterogeneity.
economics.fit: Examines whether economic constraints or selection into particular strip locations confound apparent ecological effects.

economics.method: Structured farmer interviews or surveys, potentially paired with stated-preference methods such as a discrete choice experiment, to elicit maintenance burdens, perceived risks, and incentive preferences.
economics.fit: Supplies information absent from financial records about why management differs and what subsidy features would change behavior.

economics.method: Policy-scenario or bioeconomic modeling of differentiated payments tied to location, connectivity, management standards, or ecological outcomes.
economics.fit: Tests whether the uniform subsidy is likely to support the locations and upkeep needed for ecological effectiveness.

integration.approach: Build a shared farm-by-year database linking bee observations and species traits with strip characteristics, landscape and nesting measures, pesticide timing/exposure indicators, management records, and economic variables.
integration.fit: Allows competing ecological, biological, and economic explanations to be evaluated jointly rather than in isolated disciplinary analyses.

integration.approach: Use a phased mixed-methods design: improve ecological and biological monitoring while collecting detailed cost and decision data, then use findings to evaluate alternative strip-management and subsidy scenarios.
integration.fit: Matches the existing pilot records while recognizing that causal attribution and feasible exposure testing require additional data and expert review.

required_caveats: Methods should be presented as candidate approaches, not as proof that pesticides, connectivity, economics, or any single factor caused the lack of recovery.
Sampling scale, number of farms and control edges, species-identification capacity, residue-testing feasibility, and assumptions for causal and economic models remain to be specified.
Expert review is required from ecologists, bee taxonomists/toxicologists, and agricultural economists before finalizing the design.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: Hi—sorry, I just came from the methods deadline meeting, so I’m still a bit in spreadsheets. It’s properly grey outside here too. Since we’re already running tight, can we start with what would actually separate a biological failure from a siting-and-management problem? I’m particularly worried we’re treating the strips like comparable interventions, when the edges farmers selected may have had very different costs and constraints.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: The grey weather is rather appropriate for this dataset. I think we need to record why each edge was chosen before we call a low count a biological failure. Leila, do the financial and management records say anything about the original placement decision, or only costs after planting? Ecologically, the hedge-versus-large-arable contrast is suggestive, but it could just be that farmers put strips in fundamentally different places.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: Mostly after planting, I think. The accounts are pretty aggregated, so they may show land out of production and some establishment spend, but probably not the original counterfactual, like what that particular edge was earning or the machinery inconvenience that drove selection. We need the farmers to reconstruct that, why this edge, what else was feasible, and whether the hedge edges have different upkeep or operational conflicts from the exposed ones.

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: When they reconstruct that, could we ask specifically what was already at the edge, like bare banks, hedge bases, old fence lines, that sort of thing? A hedge-adjacent strip might look better connected on a map but still have no usable nesting substrate. And I really wouldn't read the flat totals as one response. On a few of those flower-rich transects, we saw big bumblebees visiting constantly and almost no small solitary bees.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That split is important. We shouldn't make abundance the only endpoint. If the bumblebees and solitary bees respond differently, pooling them could erase both patterns. Tomás, for a realistic number of farms, which groups could we identify reliably over repeated visits, and could your nesting assessment tell us whether small bees are absent because suitable nests are missing, rather than because they just aren't using the strip...

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: At minimum, we can reliably separate bumblebees, the larger solitary bees, and the small solitary-bee complex in the field, then voucher the difficult ones for later ID. For nests, I'd score bare or lightly vegetated ground, banks, cavities in stems or deadwood, hedge bases, just whether they're there and likely suitable. Not pretend we've found every nest. If small bees are missing where those features are present, that points more toward exposure or something about the flowers, but it won't prove...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Mm, that is useful.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: And that nesting score could be attached to the actual edge, not just a farm-level landscape label? Because then we can ask whether farmers systematically put strips on low-opportunity-cost margins that also lack those features. Amina, I’m still trying to pin down whether you can map the connectivity and surrounding habitat at that same edge scale, rather than averaging it across the whole holding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Definitely. I’d map it per edge and at a few surrounding distances, rather than give the whole farm one landscape value. So immediate hedge and margin structure, then semi-natural habitat and floral resources in the wider area. The practical question is how many edge pairs, edge pairs we can support, because with only a few, we won’t be able to separate those scales from farm identity.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: And it matters that the placement decision was made back in spring 2023, before we had any outcome data. If we expand, I'd sample deliberately across those edge-scale habitat and connectivity gradients, but I'd also elicit the feasible alternative edges and their counterfactual gross margins. Otherwise the ecological comparison is still conditioned on farmers' selection. The three farms just won't carry that identification on their own.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: For 2026, I wouldn't just recruit whichever farms volunteer. We need enough farms and edge pairs to cover those placement gradients, with each planted edge paired with a genuinely comparable unplanted edge. Then we'd repeat surveys across the season and over more than one year. I can't put a number on it yet without knowing survey capacity, but three farms plainly can't support that—

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: Alongside the matching, I’d make the farmer-side data non-negotiable. We need a short structured placement interview and edge-level logs for labour, machinery detours, and adjacent-crop effects. Otherwise, an apparently equivalent control edge may not have been feasible in the farmer’s actual rotation. I’m not sure the basic accounts can support that retrospectively, especially for the route-disruption- for that one farm, the route-disruption issue.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Hm, that is a limitation.

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: And the records matter on the exposure side too. Leila, do the spray logs actually give dates and active ingredients, or are some just product names? I'd link every application to the crop and our visit dates, but a log is only an exposure history. We'd still need residue samples, if the lab capacity and detection limits make that realistic, before saying pesticides explain the small-bee- before saying they explain the small-bee pattern.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: They’re mostly product names, I think, with dates and crop blocks, but I need to check how consistently they record the active ingredients and the treated field. And yes, I wouldn’t infer exposure from the log alone. But it may still tell us whether the operational nuisance is, um, concentrating spraying right alongside particular strips, which is part of the management decision and not just a toxicology variable.

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: If spraying is concentrated beside certain strips, I’d want the timing, timing against flowering and our survey dates, not just an annual total. We could take a small, targeted set of flower or pollen samples at the contrasting edges, but I need to check what the lab can actually detect and handle before we build that into the core design.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Targeted sampling makes more sense than trying to residue-sample every edge. But when we choose those edges, we should keep the landscape contrast explicit. Otherwise a residue signal beside the large arable blocks could still be standing in for isolation, or vice versa. Could the survey visits also carry local temperature, wind, and cloud measurements? The current weather summaries are too coarse for differences in detection between exposed and hedge-side strips, and...

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: The local weather sheet needs to go with each transect visit, definitely, because small solitary bees can just vanish from counts in wind that bumblebees will still work through. I’d also record flowering stage and actual visits by group on a short fixed flower sample. Otherwise we can’t tell low detection from them being present but not, um, using the strip.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: That fixed flower sample is useful economically too, actually. If a strip has good cover but flowers only in a window that conflicts with spraying or the farmer's workable maintenance window, then "established" is hiding a real management trade-off. Could we record the maintenance operation and flowering stage together, edge by edge? I want to know whether the nuisance farmers describe is producing a systematically different floral resource, not just an unpriced...

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: Yeah, edge by edge.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: I’d add a quick vegetation record at each visit, not just flowering stage. Which species are actually open, cover, and maybe a simple continuity measure across the season. A strip can have high total cover but still have a gap in resources for the smaller solitary bees. We’re nearly out of time, but the number of visits per edge is the thing I need before fixing the landscape sample.

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: For the bee side, I’d want at least four visits, spread from early flowering through late summer. Otherwise we’ll miss the small solitary-bee peak, or mistake a floral gap for no response. The constraint is whether that’s feasible across enough edge pairs. I’d rather have fewer visits that are properly repeated than one pass over a huge sample, but Amina may need the wider spread for the landscape part.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That is a real trade-off.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: I wouldn't let wanting breadth turn this into one-visit data, because then we can't credibly connect any payment or management effect to an outcome. Maybe we do wider recruitment and placement interviews on all the candidate edges, then a stratified intensive panel with four visits and edge-level cost logs on enough contrasts to cover high- and low-opportunity-cost sites. But we need to know what the field budget actually is before we pretend that resolves...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That compromise is probably the only defensible one. The wider candidate-edge dataset can tell us if the intensive panel covers the key combinations of hedgerow connection, surrounding habitat, and farm constraints, and then the repeated counts can actually separate weather and seasonal use from a site effect. But until we have a budget and a realistic number of survey teams, I can't say whether that panel is twenty pairs or forty.

transcript.speaker: Leila M. Okafor
transcript.text: I think we should stop there and give people a few minutes back. Thanks, both. Once we’ve got a clearer sense of the budget and survey capacity, we can pick this up.

transcript.speaker: Tomás Iversen
transcript.text: Cheers, speak soon.
